notes: A running account of where things stand by these headlines, revised after each edition rather than added to. Every version is kept.
Written by the model from the narratives, not from the headlines. It is a reading, not a record.
standing: By these headlines the Iran war's price rise is now being read into the cost of borrowing: the Fed has held rates while its chair Warsh is asked about further rises, the ECB is expected to hold, South Korean mortgage rates are at a 14-year high, Russia has restricted long car loans and the UK has cut its growth forecast over the war. In Brazil, Alcolumbre plans a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro and Flávio Bolsonaro has reached the United States with Trump's consent, while in South Korea former president Yoon Suk Yeol faces a second death sentence. AI data centres are lifting profits at Samsung and Taiwan's CHPT while Norway's parliament considers an urgent freeze, a Finnish city faces a police report over cleared forest and Russian data centres are under attack. A high-speed collision near Urda in Spain that killed 68 people followed at least 15 signalling warnings, and a JR train in Japan overran a station when its automatic braking did not act. Student strikes, housing protests and failing public schemes, reported on 27 October, had no narrative on 29 October.
moved: The Iran and fuel thread moved from jet fuel, asphalt and subsidy rules on 27 October to central bank holds and mortgage and loan rates in South Korea, Japan and Russia on 29 October; only the UK growth forecast in that evidence names the war.

Brazil's events moved on without a narrative of their own: Flávio Bolsonaro is reported to have reached the United States with Trump's consent and Alcolumbre plans a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro, both carried on 29 October in a new thread on former leaders beside Yoon Suk Yeol's second death sentence.

Data centres returned on 29 October apart from AI companies' listing and lawsuits, as profit in Korea and Taiwan and as planning and security disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia, and now form their own thread.
A new thread began on failed safety systems, led by the Urda rail collision in Spain after repeated signalling warnings.
silent: Four single-observation threads from early 27 October are now silent: money leaving into dollars and gold, AI buyouts beside dangerous manual work, rites counted before the days of the dead, and European household readiness beside borrowed warheads. None was linked to anything after it, so this may as much reflect each edition writing fresh joins as the world moving on.

Students striking and occupying, and state housing drives with housing protests, have had no narrative since the morning of 27 October. The editions given include none stamped 28 October, so a day of headlines is missing from view and the strikes may have grown or ended unseen.

Drones as one machine, the football night and courts re-sentencing past events remain silent since 26 October, partly because the first edition's figurative joins have not been the kind later editions write.

threads.label: Iran war, Hormuz, fuel and borrowing costs
threads.text: On 26 October the join was the Gulf running talks and strike preparations side by side. On the morning of 27 October it was the Hormuz oil shock raising US petrol and European gas prices while Iran hosted Gulf security talks. By that evening it had reached jet fuel, with US airlines charging about 23% more, an easyJet flight leaving Naples without luggage, Estonia out of asphalt, and fuel and power rules changing in Malaysia, India, Ukraine and South Korea. On 29 October it reached borrowing: the Fed held with chair Warsh asked about further rises, the ECB was expected to hold, South Korean mortgage rates hit a 14-year high, Hiroshima borrowers moved to fixed rates, Russia restricted long car loans and the UK cut its growth forecast. Only the UK item names Iran.
threads.direction: It has moved outward from diplomacy to the pump, to refined products and now to central bank rates and loan contracts, with the war named less often at each step.

threads.label: Brazil's election and the United States
threads.text: On 26 October the join was Brazil's vote being read as a script in Buenos Aires, Madrid and Nairobi. On the morning of 27 October it narrowed to Trump calling the election rigged while offering $1 million for evidence of fraud in US elections. By that evening, after Lula's run-off win, the United States was the common party: Flávio Bolsonaro reported travelling there with talk of asylum, Lula warning of persecution and foreign money, about 300 US soldiers arriving in Colombia, and Machado returning to Venezuela. No narrative carried this thread on 29 October, but its events reappeared in the former-leaders thread: Flávio Bolsonaro reported reaching the United States with Trump's consent, and Alcolumbre planning a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro.
threads.direction: It has moved from how Brazil's vote is read abroad to Washington's part in what follows, and on 29 October its events were taken up under a wider join about former leaders.

threads.label: AI companies' listing, land and lawsuits
threads.text: On 26 October the join was an AI company listing the end of the world as a risk factor in its prospectus and the market buying the shares. Early on 27 October an edition followed data centres down to county level, where land, grid and water requests were being refused. On the morning of 27 October Anthropic filed for a record US share listing as Elvis Presley's rights holders sued it over 200 songs. The first Chronicle joined these into one thread. On 29 October data centres returned without the listing or the lawsuits and now have their own thread; the county narrative stays here because earlier narratives keep their threads. No narrative on the companies' listing or courts has appeared in the two editions since.
threads.direction: It has gone from the prospectus to the ground and the courts, and the data-centre ground has since split away into its own thread.

threads.label: Students striking and occupying
threads.text: On 26 October the join was young people in public squares: students had brought down a government, and a president was copying a teenage dance. On the morning of 27 October it became concrete, with students on strike or occupying buildings in France, Mexico, India and Italy, Serbia expected next, and police action at universities in the frame. No narrative has carried it in the two editions since, on the evening of 27 October and on 29 October, so whether the strikes grew or ended is not shown by these headlines. One more edition without it and it turns silent.
threads.direction: It moved from youth as a political image to named strikes and occupations, then went unmentioned for two editions.

threads.label: State housing drives and housing protests
threads.text: On the morning of 27 October one narrative joined Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu expanding housing through states and employers with Portugal investigating police conduct at housing protests, and the part property funds play. It set state building programmes beside street protest over the cost of a home. No narrative followed it on the evening of 27 October or on 29 October, though the 29 October rise in Korean and Japanese mortgage rates bears on the same households by these headlines.

threads.label: Public schemes passing costs to households
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. In six countries a public scheme meant to cover a cost was reported as falling short: Canadians paying for private surgery from savings and GoFundMe, German adult children billed for parents' care, Lucknow's subsidised generic pharmacies short of medicines, a Bangladeshi antivenom programme lacking funds, compensation claims from 50,000 Australians over unlawful Centrelink suspensions, and doubt over a Mexican voluntary pension scheme. The case against noted that several of these stories have run for years and one is a wealth-advice column. No narrative carried it on 29 October.

threads.label: AI-made faces and files in checks
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. Nigeria's electoral commission is investigating suspected AI-generated photos in the voters' register, New Zealand job seekers report being ignored as AI-written applications flood employers, an Australian court passed the first sentence under deepfake laws without jail, and fashion models face AI copies of their image. The join is that a plausible picture or document now costs little to make while checking it still takes a person's time. Several cited cases, in Japan, the Philippines and Ghana, use methods older than generative software. No narrative carried it on 29 October.

threads.label: Broadcasts and films removed over offence
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. A Chinese platform dropped Racing-Real Madrid and La Liga broadcasts were suspended after a remark by Mbappé, an Indian court ordered a documentary on Adani and Modi taken down, a Korean drama faced calls to halt over a Gwangju episode, and Neil Young sued to stop Trump rallies using his songs, while police in Jordan, Egypt and Spain acted against content and a Mexican court struck down a state propaganda law. Three of the headlines were the same Mbappé story from different countries. No narrative carried it on 29 October.

threads.label: AI data centres as profit, dispute and target
threads.text: Begun on 29 October. Samsung's battery and IT units and Taiwan's CHPT reported sharply higher profits on AI data centre demand, while Norway's parliament considered an urgent freeze on data centres, a Finnish city faced a police report for clearing forest for one, and Cloud.ru planned reserve capacity as Russian data centres came under attack. The join is one kind of building seen as profit, as a claim on land and power, and as a military target. The case against notes that Samsung SDI's gain may be energy storage, the Norwegian freeze may be aimed at crypto-mining, and the objections come only from Nordic and Russian outlets. It follows ground first covered on 27 October in the county narrative kept in the AI industry thread.

threads.label: Former leaders between courts and amnesty
threads.text: Begun on 29 October. South Korea's special counsel again sought, and by one report won, a death sentence for former president Yoon Suk Yeol over his martial law declaration, while in Brazil Alcolumbre planned a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro and Flávio Bolsonaro reached the United States with Trump's consent. An expert report contradicted Spain's Zapatero over jewels, India seized Azam Khan's university and Indonesia's parliament opened its anti-corruption law to revision. The join is a former office-holder's case being settled by a court or by politics. Two cases concern seizures of power and the rest money, and the Brazilian events also belong to the run of the Brazil thread.

threads.label: Failed safety systems and operator blame
threads.text: Begun on 29 October and marked tentative by its own edition. A high-speed collision near Urda in Spain, which other headlines say killed 68 people, followed at least 15 warnings about faulty signalling; a JR train in Japan overran a station when its driver was drowsy and its automatic braking did not act; Bangladesh is investigating a grid failure and a three-hour identity server outage; Manila's airport has broken CCTVs; and Mexico lost internet across several networks. The join is a safety layer that was itself not working, with first official blame on the operator. Only the Spanish and Japanese cases have a stated cause, and half the evidence is Spanish.

threads.label: Money leaving and states offering discounts
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined savings and fortunes moving into dollars, gold and trusts with states answering by amnesties and discounts meant to bring the money back into view. No narrative in the three editions since has followed it, so it stands as a single observation. The former-leaders thread of 29 October mentions amnesty bills, but those concern convictions, not tax or hidden money.

threads.label: AI buyouts and dangerous manual work
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative set office workers being paid to leave as AI takes their tasks against labourers still dying in ditches, fields and collapsed buildings: a buyout for the clerk and an accident for the manual worker. No later narrative has carried it in three editions. AI has appeared since in other joins, fakes in checks on 27 October and data centres on 29 October, but not as a matter of jobs.

threads.label: Rites counted before the days of the dead
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined reports that measured the rites of late October and early November before they happen: numbers of hosts, incense sticks, costumes and the strain on worshippers' knees. It was a seasonal join and no narrative has carried it in the three editions since. With Halloween and the days of the dead still ahead on 31 October and 1 and 2 November, it may return.

threads.label: European household readiness and borrowed deterrence
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined European advice that households should be able to last 72 hours on their own with European states seeking cover from nuclear warheads they do not themselves own. The join placed civil preparation at the kitchen-cupboard level beside talk of extended deterrence between states. No narrative in the three editions since has returned to it, so it stands as a single observation.

threads.label: Drones doing many civil and military jobs
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined drones cutting power, guarding a lake, carrying the wounded and being sold, treating one kind of machine as the common object across war, policing, rescue and trade. No narrative has carried it in the four editions since. Attacks on Russian data centres on 29 October, described there as part of a drone campaign, sit in a different thread.

threads.label: One football night watched worldwide
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined coverage of a single football night that drew attention across many countries at once. It was tied to one event and no narrative has carried it in the four editions since. Football returned on 27 October only as a broadcasting dispute in the removal-over-offence thread, and not at all on 29 October.

threads.label: Courts re-sentencing past events
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined courts re-sentencing events of 1979 and 1996 with a library removing material from 2026, treating them as revisions of the record. No narrative has carried it in the four editions since. The Korean drama over Gwangju on 27 October and the former-leaders thread begun on 29 October touch nearby ground, but neither re-sentences an old event.

withdrawn.held: AI companies' share listings, the copyright suit against Anthropic and county refusals of data centre land, grid and water formed one thread.
withdrawn.undone: On 29 October data centres returned on their own, as profit for Samsung and CHPT and as planning and security disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia, with no listing or lawsuit in view. The land and power question is running apart from the companies' finance and courts, so the merge no longer holds.

caseAgainst: This Chronicle rests on five editions over about 53 hours, and the editions given include none stamped 28 October, so the step from 27 to 29 October hides a day of headlines and cannot show what happened between. Only one narrative in all five editions carries a formal continuation link, the mortgage narrative's link to the fuel narrative, and the brief that asks for continuity may have produced that link as much as the world did: the evidence for the war reaching borrowing costs is mostly headlines that do not name Iran, and the edition's own case against says the rise in rates can be explained as inflation left over from 2022. I kept the data centre and Bolsonaro events out of their earlier threads because they carried no link, and a reader could fairly have joined them; I also withdrew my own earlier merge of the AI thread, which shows how much the threads depend on my grouping. The sample shapes today directly: the data centre objections come only from Nordic and Russian outlets, half the backup-systems evidence is Spanish, and the previous Chronicle's view of the fuel shock as the leading thread may have pulled me to place it first again.
line: On 29 October 2026 the Iran war's price rise is read into borrowing costs: the Fed holds, Korean mortgage rates hit a 14-year high, and the UK cuts growth over the war.
revision: Three threads begun, on data centres, former leaders and failed safety systems, the Iran fuel thread extended to borrowing costs, and four single-observation threads from early 27 October marked silent, leaving eleven live. The first version's merge of data centres into the AI industry thread is withdrawn, and its count of live threads is corrected: it had twelve, not thirteen. The standing was rewritten around borrowing costs, Brazil's amnesty and exit, data centres and the Urda collision.
